question.text: Is bicompartmental knee arthroplasty more favourable to knee muscle strength and physical performance compared to total knee arthroplasty?
question.context: Bicompartmental knee arthroplasty features bone and ligament sparing as unicompartmental knee arthroplasty and is presumably better in the recovery of muscle strength and function compared to total knee arthroplasty (TKA) though not previously reported in the literature. The aim of the study was to compare isokinetic knee muscle strength and physical performance in patients who underwent either bicompartmental knee arthroplasty or TKA. Each of 24 patients (31 knees) was prospectively examined preoperatively, at 6 and 12 months after each surgery. Isokinetic knee extensor and flexor strength as well as position sense were measured using the Biodex system. Timed up and go test, stair climbing test, and the 6-min walk test were used to assess physical performance. The results of each group were also compared with those from the corresponding healthy control, respectively. Demography showed significant difference in the mean age between bicompartment (54.8 ± 5.6 years) and TKA groups (65.7 ± 6.7 years). Comparing between the two groups, knee extensor and flexor torque, hamstring/Quadriceps ratio, position sense, and physical performance were not significantly different preoperatively, at 6 and 12 months after surgery. In intra-group analysis, muscle strength and position sense at each time point were not different in both groups. In physical performance, both groups resulted in improvement in the 6-min walk test, and only TKA group showed enhancement in stair climbing test.

medgemma_4b.clinical_reasoning: The study found no significant difference in knee extensor and flexor torque, hamstring/Quadriceps ratio, position sense, or physical performance between the bicompartmental knee arthroplasty and total knee arthroplasty groups at any time point (preoperative, 6 months, or 12 months). The TKA group showed improvement in stair climbing test, while the bicompartmental group showed improvement in the 6-min walk test.
medgemma_4b.critical_evidence: The study found no significant difference in knee extensor and flexor torque, hamstring/Quadriceps ratio, position sense, or physical performance between the bicompartmental knee arthroplasty and total knee arthroplasty groups at any time point (preoperative, 6 months, or 12 months).
medgemma_4b.differential_considered: While the study did not directly compare muscle strength and physical performance, the lack of significant differences between the two groups suggests that bicompartmental knee arthroplasty is not necessarily more favorable in this regard. The improvement in stair climbing test in the TKA group could be due to the more extensive joint replacement, which may provide better stability and proprioception for this activity.

rnj1_8b.clinical_reasoning: The study found no significant differences in muscle strength or physical performance between bicompartmental knee arthroplasty and total knee arthroplasty at 6 and 12 months postoperatively. While both groups showed improvements in the 6-min walk test, only the TKA group showed enhancement in stair climbing, suggesting TKA may have a slight edge in certain physical performance measures. The lack of significant differences in key outcomes like muscle strength and position sense between the two procedures indicates that bicompartmental arthroplasty is not superior to TKA in terms of muscle strength and physical performance.
rnj1_8b.critical_evidence: The study found no significant differences in knee extensor and flexor torque, hamstring/Quadriceps ratio, position sense, and physical performance between the two groups at 6 and 12 months postoperatively.
rnj1_8b.differential_considered: No differential diagnoses were relevant to this question as it focuses on comparing surgical outcomes. The key consideration was the lack of significant differences between the two procedures in muscle strength and physical performance, which directly addresses the clinical question.

qwen3_vl_8b.clinical_reasoning: The study found no significant differences in isokinetic muscle strength, position sense, or physical performance between bicompartmental knee arthroplasty and TKA at any time point, including 6 and 12 months post-op. Although bicompartmental arthroplasty is theoretically advantageous due to bone and ligament sparing, the data do not support superior outcomes in muscle strength or physical performance compared to TKA.
qwen3_vl_8b.critical_evidence: Comparing between the two groups, knee extensor and flexor torque, hamstring/Quadriceps ratio, position sense, and physical performance were not significantly different preoperatively, at 6 and 12 months after surgery.
qwen3_vl_8b.differential_considered: The theoretical advantage of bicompartmental arthroplasty was considered, but the study's objective measurements showed no significant difference in outcomes, ruling out superiority.

olmo3_7b.critical_evidence: Knee extensor and flexor torque, hamstring/quadriceps ratio, position sense, and 6-min walk test results were not significantly different between the bicompartmental and TKA groups at 6 or 12 months postoperatively.
olmo3_7b.differential_considered: I considered whether age-related differences or surgical technique (bone and ligament sparing in bicompartmental vs. total replacement in TKA) could affect recovery, but the lack of significant differences in muscle strength and physical performance between groups at follow-up suggests that any such factors are not reflected in the measured outcomes in this study.
